title: Methodological approaches and main factors considered in school soundscape studies: A scoping review
authors: Hatice Kubra Kurukose Cal et al., 2024
review_question: Which age groups are mostly studied in school soundscape literature, and which are underrepresented? What sound sources are usually studied in school soundscape literature and how sounds are perceived by people? What are common methodological approaches implemented in school soundscape studies?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Included studies investigated schools' spaces/facilities and occupants' perceptions of the sound environment. Excluded studies assessed only acoustic parameters (e.g., speech clarity, reverberation time, speech transmission index) or used only data other than people's perception.

findings.antecedent: Age group of participants in school soundscape studies
findings.quote: Mostly, primary school-aged children have been involved as participants in soundscape studies.

findings.antecedent: Sound sources investigated in school soundscape studies
findings.quote: Nearly half of reviewed studies investigated negative sounds which are mostly coming from outside of the school facilities (e.g. traffic noise).

findings.consequent: Distress caused by insufficient acoustic comfort
findings.quote: School soundscape studies commonly focus on the distress caused by insufficient levels of acoustic comfort.

findings.antecedent: Methodologies used in school soundscape studies
findings.quote: School soundscape studies used combined methodologies for more reliable results. Interviews and questionnaires were the most common methodological approaches.

synthesis_conclusions: The acoustic environments children are exposed to in school facilities are of utmost importance for their physical and mental health, overall well-being, and cognitive development.
Traditionally, acoustic-related studies in schools focused on room acoustics performance for speech-related parameters (e.g., speech intelligibility, reverberation time, background noise level).
School designers and facility managers should acknowledge a more holistic effect of soundscapes on school health, considering the overall sonic experience of the school premises.
Primary school-aged children are the most common participants in soundscape studies.
Nearly half of reviewed studies investigated negative sounds, primarily traffic noise, originating from outside school facilities.
School soundscape studies commonly focus on the distress caused by insufficient levels of acoustic comfort.
Combined methodologies, particularly interviews and questionnaires, are the most common approaches in school soundscape studies for more reliable results.
evidence_gaps: Need to consider secondary school children's perceptions in soundscape studies.
Scarcity of research investigating the potential of restorative sounds in designing acoustic environments.
Lack of studies investigating the school's sound environment as a whole.
Limited attention on children's own assessments and judgment in school acoustic literature.
Need for research into the positive aspects of school soundscapes and their influence on multisensory learning experiences.
Limited number of studies examining indoor environments, especially for schools.
Soundscape studies have primarily centered around urban environments.
limitations: Soundscape studies on specific building types are restricted, with few focusing on indoor school environments.
Primary reliance on the Scopus database may lead to omission of relevant literature from other databases.
Exclusion of articles not written in English may lead to the exclusion of valuable research.
Strictness of the search string might have excluded some relevant articles.
Potential for bias in the study selection process, despite multiple reviewers.

paper_metadata.title: Methodological approaches and main factors considered in school soundscape studies: A scoping review
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Methodological approaches and main factors considered in school soundscape studies: A scoping review
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: School acoustics is pivotal for children’s well-being given their substantial time commitment to education within these environments, with potential positive or negative impacts. Soundscape has gained relevance in various settings, including indoor environments, and explores both positive and negative responses of individuals to sounds within a context. This scoping review aims to investigate the application of the soundscape approach within the school environment, with a primary focus on evaluating perceptions of the acoustic environment. It aims to identify key factors considered in the studies, such as age groups, sound sources, and methodologies. A Scopus search was conducted, covering the period from January 2000 to September 2023. The search was limited to peer-reviewed articles published in English. The inclusion criteria required studies to investigate schools and assess the perceptions. After screening, 11 studies met the inclusion criteria from 49 articles. The most targeted age cohort was primary school-aged children. Yet, the need to consider secondary school children’s perceptions persists. The dominant sounds investigated were categorized as “negative” sounds, referring to auditory stimuli that are commonly perceived as unpleasant. These negative sounds were primarily traffic-induced noise. The prevailing method used was questionnaires. To advance school soundscape research, exploring secondary school-aged children’s views would provide valuable insights. By enhancing knowledge in this field, researchers can improve school acoustics for student well-being. Notably, a limitation of this review is that soundscape studies have centered around urban environments so far. Consequently, there have been only a limited number of studies examining indoor environments, and even less for schools.
